title: What is trauma?
citation: Bisson, J. I., Cosgrove, S., Lewis, C., & Roberts, N. P. (2015). Post-traumatic stress disorder. Bmj, 351.
content:
What is trauma?

Trauma is the emotional and physical response to an event, or series of events, that feels overwhelming or threatens a person's sense of safety. Traumatic experiences can include accidents, violence, abuse, serious illness, loss, natural disasters, or ongoing situations where a person feels trapped, powerless, or constantly unsafe. What makes an experience traumatic is how the brain and body respond to it. Two people can experience the same event and be affected very differently.

Isn't trauma only caused by one major, obvious event?

A common misconception is that trauma only comes from extreme events such as war or major disasters. While these experiences can certainly be traumatic, trauma can also develop after repeated or ongoing experiences such as childhood neglect, bullying, domestic abuse, discrimination, or living in an unpredictable environment. The impact depends on factors such as age, previous experiences, available support and how safe the person felt during and after the event, rather than on the event alone.

Why does my body react as if the danger is still happening?

Trauma can change the way the brain and nervous system respond to potential threats. During a traumatic experience, the body's survival system prepares to fight, flee, or freeze. For some people, this system remains highly sensitive even after the danger has passed. The brain may continue scanning for signs of threat, while the body stays on high alert. This is why someone may startle easily, feel constantly tense, have trouble sleeping, or react strongly to reminders that seem harmless to others.

What are flashbacks and intrusive memories?

One of the hallmark experiences of trauma is the return of unwanted memories. Intrusive memories can appear suddenly, often triggered by sights, sounds, smells, places, or situations that remind the brain of the original event. Sometimes these memories feel so vivid that it can seem as though the event is happening again. These experiences are known as flashbacks. They are not a sign that someone is losing touch with reality, but rather that the brain has not fully processed the traumatic memory in the same way as ordinary memories.

Trauma vs difficult memory: what's the difference?

Most people have memories of difficult or upsetting experiences that become less emotionally intense over time. Traumatic memories often behave differently. They can remain vivid, emotionally charged and easily triggered long after the event has ended. Rather than feeling like something that happened in the past, traumatic memories can feel as though they are happening in the present. This ongoing sense of threat is what often distinguishes trauma from an ordinary difficult memory.

Why does this still affect me when it happened so long ago?

Many people feel frustrated or confused when trauma continues to affect them years after the event. This happens because the brain's survival system is designed to prioritise safety over the accurate recording of time. Until the traumatic memory has been fully processed, reminders can continue to trigger the same emotional and physical reactions that occurred during the original event. The passage of time alone does not always reduce these responses and needing longer to recover does not mean someone is weak or stuck.

When should I get support for trauma?

It is worth seeking support if memories of a traumatic experience continue to feel overwhelming, frequently return without warning, or interfere with work, relationships, sleep, or daily life. Effective treatments are available that help the brain process traumatic memories and reduce the ongoing sense of threat. Many people notice significant improvements with evidence-based psychological therapies and recovery is possible even when the traumatic event happened many years ago.
